headline: Intel's warning and AI-capex jitters jar an otherwise strong earnings season
body: Stocks closed out October with their worst session since June: the S&P 500 fell 1.82% to 7,580, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.86%, and the Dow slipped 1.09%, leaving the week down roughly 0.6%-2% across the three indices. The proximate trigger was Intel, which beat third-quarter estimates but tumbled near 30% on a weak forward outlook, while Amazon's results reignited worries that aggressive AI-infrastructure spending is outrunning near-term payoff even though the company's own numbers beat expectations. That sits against a Fed that held rates at 3.75%-4.00% on October 28 by a 10-2 vote, with the two dissenters pushing for a hike rather than a cut — futures markets now price roughly 80% odds of a December hike, a notably hawkish repricing for a market that spent most of the year leaning toward cuts.

The cross-asset reaction looks more like a capex-specific unwind than a classic flight to safety: gold slid to a one-year low and bitcoin weakened alongside equities rather than catching a safe-haven bid, suggesting investors were paring risk broadly rather than rotating into traditional hedges. Underneath the volatility, the fundamental backdrop remains unusually strong — S&P 500 companies are tracking more than 30% year-over-year earnings growth for the quarter — which argues the pullback reads more as a reassessment of AI-spending and rate-path assumptions than a broader growth scare. Retail-sentiment chatter was thin and inconclusive heading into the weekend, so this read leans more on price action and the Fed/earnings news flow than on any clear social-sentiment signal.
